audits.mathematicalReason: Let M be the midpoint of AB and the common tangency point of circles A and B. Since the radii are 1, AM=BM=CM=1, and tangency of circle C to AB gives CM perpendicular to AB. For circles A and C, their other intersection together with A, M, and C forms a unit square. Thus their overlap consists of two 90° sectors minus that square, with area π/2−1. The overlap with circle B has the same area. Because circles A and B have disjoint interiors, these two overlap areas can be subtracted without double-counting: π−2(π/2−1)=2. The candidate scopes correctly describe this valid sector-and-square method.
